article.overview: A regolith beneficiation system is equipment that sorts lunar regolith into fractions with different mineral content, so that a chosen mineral (for example ilmenite, which contains iron and titanium oxides, or anorthite, a calcium-aluminium feldspar) can be concentrated before further processing. Beneficiation does not extract oxygen or metal by itself. It is a preparation step that could reduce the mass of material sent to downstream extraction or construction processes. The published work reviewed here uses physical separation methods: sieving, permanent-magnet separation and electrostatic (tribocharging) separation. The most detailed verified study is a laboratory testbed at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) that used lunar regolith simulants. Electrostatic beneficiation has also been tested in reduced-gravity aircraft flights. No lunar-surface demonstration was found in the sources reviewed.
article.description: The term 'regolith beneficiation system' describes a class of ISRU processing hardware rather than one standard flight instrument. A typical system would include a feed system that meters regolith into the separator; a particle-size stage, such as a sieve, to remove oversize particles; a magnetic stage that removes or collects strongly magnetic minerals; an electrostatic stage that charges particles by contact and deflects them according to their electrical behaviour; collection bins or outlets that separate the enriched and depleted fractions; and control electronics and, for a flight or surface system, power, thermal control and dust protection. The published systems described in this article combine several of these stages. Their performance figures depend on the simulant, the particle size range, the feed rate and the separator settings, and cannot be transferred directly to a different design or to real lunar regolith without testing.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of beneficiation in lunar ISRU is to increase the concentration of a useful mineral in the feed material. Ilmenite is of interest because it contains iron and titanium and has been studied as a feedstock for oxygen production. Anorthite is of interest because a high-purity fraction could be a feedstock for structural materials such as sintered or cast ceramics. In the sources reviewed, the target minerals differ between studies: the DLR work focuses on ilmenite, the Bachle et al. (2025) design describes aluminium-, iron-titanium- and magnesium-iron-bearing product fractions, and the Coffman et al. (2026) work targets anorthite. Beneficiation could also remove unwanted fine dust or classify particles by size before further processing. These applications are proposed in the sources; none has been shown to operate as part of a complete lunar oxygen or construction chain in the sources reviewed.
article.operating_principle: Beneficiation depends on differences in physical properties between minerals in regolith. Particle size is separated by a sieve or sizing stage. Magnetic susceptibility allows strongly magnetic grains, such as those rich in ilmenite, to be deflected by a permanent-magnet drum or a magnetic field. Triboelectric (contact) charging causes minerals to acquire different electrical charges when they rub against each other or a surface; charged particles can then be deflected by an electric field, a process called tribocharging or electrostatic separation. In the DLR testbed described by Kulkarni et al. (2024), a sieve removed particles larger than 200 µm, a permanent-magnet drum separator removed ferromagnetic material, and a parallel-plate tribocharging separator operated at an optimised field voltage of 14 kV separated the remaining material. In the Bachle et al. (2025) design, the magnetic and electrostatic stages are integrated into one unit, and the electrostatic sieving stage is described as driven by a square wave at 1.8–2.5 kV peak and 5–40 Hz. Enrichment compares the target mineral concentration in the output with that in the input; recovery describes how much of the target mineral in the feed is captured in the enriched output. A high enrichment ratio with low recovery can still be a poor process, so both values must be considered together.
article.scientific_importance: Regolith beneficiation matters for lunar science and resource use because the composition of regolith varies with location, age and grain size. Studies of how minerals separate under lunar-like conditions show which processes could work in practice and which assumptions are most uncertain. The reviewed sources also show that results obtained in laboratory simulant tests, in aircraft flights and in vacuum chambers are not directly interchangeable. Measuring the effect of gravity and vacuum on separation is therefore an important scientific and engineering question.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal mass, size or power requirement for a regolith beneficiation system. The examples below describe specific laboratory, aircraft-test or design configurations. Where a value was not found in a verified source, it is recorded as null or 'not publicly specified'. Performance values are tied to the simulant and configuration in each example.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The verified sources do not give a complete dimensional description of a flight-representative beneficiation system. Dimensions for the DLR testbed, the aircraft apparatus and the Bachle unit are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. A surface system's dimensions would need to be set by its feed rate, separation stages, and mounting and dust-protection requirements.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not publicly specified for any beneficiation system reviewed. For spacecraft engineering, mass is normally expressed in kilograms, and it governs launch and lander capacity, structural support and deployment design. A flight system's mass cannot be estimated from the laboratory or aircraft examples.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not publicly specified for any beneficiation system reviewed, apart from the electrostatic stage voltages described above (14 kV in the DLR testbed; 1.8 to 2.5 kV peak square wave in the Bachle et al. design). Electrical power consumption, thermal load and heating requirements are not verified.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar beneficiation system would have to operate with the same environmental constraints as other surface hardware: vacuum, very large temperature swings, abrasive fine dust and reduced gravity. Some of these conditions have been tested in part. Electrostatic separation depends on charge behaviour, humidity, dust adhesion and particle-surface contact, all of which may depend on vacuum and gravity. The aircraft tests cover 1/6 g for short periods but not a full lunar environment. The laboratory simulant tests do not cover the full range of real regolith properties, including glassy and agglutinate particles found in actual lunar soil. Operationally, a surface system would need a feed source (for example excavated regolith), power, thermal control, dust protection and a way to collect or transfer the enriched product. These are engineering considerations and are not verified for any specific system.
article.limitations: The most detailed verified results come from simulant tests, not from real lunar regolith. Enrichment ratios and recovery values depend on the simulant, the input-grade baseline and the separator settings. The DLR paper's input values are inconsistent within the paper, and the aircraft-flight figures are taken from an abstract excerpt. Gravity and vacuum affect electrostatic separation, and their effects have only been partly tested. Recovery and throughput are not the same as enrichment; some reported systems have low yield or recovery, which limits their use for a complete process. Beneficiation produces an enriched fraction and a depleted fraction, and the use of the depleted material is not addressed in the reviewed sources.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A surface regolith beneficiation system would be delivered as part of a lunar lander payload or a surface processing package. The verified sources do not describe a specific lander, rover or delivery mission for any beneficiation hardware, so no compatibility claim is made.
transportation_process: Integrate the beneficiation hardware into a spacecraft or lander payload compartment on Earth.
Launch it into space using a launch vehicle.
Use a lunar lander to deliver it to the surface.
Deploy and set up the system, then connect its power, data, thermal and mechanical interfaces.
Supply regolith feed to the system and collect the enriched and depleted fractions.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not publicly specified for any beneficiation system in the sources reviewed. Possible approaches include a robotic excavator feeding the system or manual handling in an early demonstration, but these are not verified options for any specific mission.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The reduced-gravity aircraft flights described by Quinn et al. are the closest flight-environment tests found; they were not spaceflight. The DLR testbed is a laboratory system. No lunar-surface beneficiation operation was verified in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: A future system's compatibility with a lander would need to be assessed using its mass, dimensions, mounting points, landing loads, power, thermal interfaces, dust protection and feed-supply method. No such assessment is possible from the sources reviewed, and no lander compatibility is asserted.

article.historical_significance: Earlier work on electrostatic separation of lunar simulant at NASA's Kennedy Space Center is recorded in a NASA NTRS entry (accession 20110016172; full text not readable in this review). Search snippets summarise that work as reaching ilmenite enrichment of up to 200% [6]; this figure is unverified. Secondary summaries also describe earlier vacuum work reaching enrichment of up to a few hundred percent; the primary paper was not read. The Quinn et al. aircraft work [2] (year not verified in full text) is significant because it moves the process from ground testing toward a reduced-gravity environment. The 2024 DLR work [1] provides a documented laboratory testbed with stated settings and enrichment values, while the 2025 and 2026 AIAA papers [3][4] describe newer integrated magnetic-electrostatic systems, with results that are preliminary or not yet verified in this review.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Technology readiness: the DLR paper reports TRL 4 for its testbed; no system reviewed is described as flight-qualified or flown in space. Simulant dependence: all reviewed quantitative results use lunar simulants (LMS-1, TMIA4, NU-LHT-2M or similar), whose composition may not match real lunar regolith, especially fine dust and agglutinates. Input-grade inconsistency: the DLR paper reports two different input-grade baselines, and the enrichment ratio depends on which is used. Aircraft-flight data: the 65% and 106% enrichment figures are from an abstract excerpt; per-flight voltages, sample sizes and statistical details were not verified. Newer AIAA papers: the Bachle et al. (2025) abstract reports design parameters only, and the Coffman et al. (2026) abstract reports preliminary results without numerical values. Secondary claims not verified: a Missouri S&T / NASA LuSTR project summary describing a parabolic-flight campaign and a TRL change to 6 could not be read and is not used in this article. Unverified mass, power and dimensions: no verified data are available for any beneficiation system reviewed. Full-text gaps: full texts of the Quinn, Bachle and Coffman papers were not read, and several sources returned binary or access-restricted content.
